new_statements.quote: The data for Man Met phonology was recorded by Chen (2005) from native speakers of the Xiao Mammi village (小曼咪村), Jinghong County, Xishuangbanna, Yunnan. [...] Most lexemes are monosyllabic, though disyllabic compound words are pretty common. Stress falls on the final syllable in disyllables. The word structure can be described as (ʔa/m).ˈCiV(Cf)T. [...] Man Met features seven tones, though some one them have limited distributions.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (en.wikipedia 'Man Met language', revision 1361714230). All three quoted fragments are there verbatim: the Phonology lead ('The data for Man Met phonology was recorded by Chen (2005) from native speakers of the Xiao Mammi village (小曼咪村), Jinghong County, Xishuangbanna, Yunnan.'), the whole Word structure paragraph ('Most lexemes are monosyllabic, though disyllabic compound words are pretty common. Stress falls on the final syllable in disyllables. The word structure can be described as (ʔa/m).ˈCiV(Cf)T.') and the tones sentence ('Man Met features seven tones, though some one them have limited distributions.'). One correction to the locator: the Word structure paragraph carries NO foo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are mostly monosyllabic; in disyllables (sesquisyllables with a presyllable ʔa- or m- before the main syllable, and disyllabic compounds) stress falls on the final syllable, i.e. on the tone-bearing main syllable. First-hand support from Chen 2005 (Google Books snippet) is only structural: the word has a major syllable and a minor syllable, the minor-syllable system being limited to the prefix a and syllabic m; no explicit stress sentence was located in Chen 2005's indexed text.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; words of more than two syllables not discussed (Chen 2005 says multisyllabic words beyond two syllables are few).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms; the language is tonal (7 tones per Chen 2005 / Sidwell 2015), so stress is a phonetic prominence on the main syllable rather than a contrastive accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog kemi1240 'Kemiehua' (ISO 639-3 kfj) is a RETIRED bookkeeping entry: the Glottolog page (downloaded 2026-09-17) says Chen Guoqing 2005 shows it to be the same language as Man Met [mml] = Glottolog manm1238 (Austroasiatic > Palaungic > Angkuic), spoken in Jinghong, Xishuangbanna, Yunnan. Man Met/Kemie is already in our catalog as manm1238 (Wikipedia-derived, fixed-unreviewed); kemi1240 should be merged into that record, not catalogued separately. Chen 2005's description is of the Xiaomanmi village (小曼咪村) variety.
